posts.title: MCP is the new middleware
posts.hook: MCP servers are becoming the plumbing layer nobody planned for.
posts.body:
MCP servers are becoming the plumbing layer nobody planned for.

I wired four of them into a single agent loop last month. Research, drafting, scheduling, CRM updates. One prompt kicks it off, four servers do the work.

The part that surprised me: the hard problem isn't connecting them. It's the handoff between them.

Server A returns a company object. Server B expects a domain string. Server C wants a JSON blob with fields Server A doesn't produce. You spend 80% of your time writing glue logic to translate between tools that supposedly speak the same protocol.

Sound familiar? It should. This is the exact same integration tax we paid with REST APIs for a decade. Different envelope, same problem.

The teams winning right now aren't the ones with the most MCP servers connected. They're the ones who standardized their internal data shapes first, then plugged servers in.

I keep a single canonical record format in SQLite. Every MCP server's output gets normalized into that shape before anything downstream touches it. Boring? Absolutely. But my agent loops don't break when I swap out a provider.

The protocol isn't the moat. The data contract between your tools is.

remixes.label: plumbing-over-prompting
remixes.hook: The best prompt engineers I know aren't writing prompts anymore. They're writing glue code between MCP servers.
remixes.body:
The best prompt engineers I know aren't writing prompts anymore. They're writing glue code between MCP servers.

Here's what happened. I had an agent that researched prospects, drafted outreach, scheduled sends, and logged everything to a CRM. Four distinct tools. One loop.

The prompt was maybe 40 lines. The schema translation layer between servers was 400.

Server A returns a nested company object with 15 fields. Server B wants a flat string. Server C expects an ISO timestamp that Server D emits as Unix epoch. Every integration point is a type mismatch waiting to happen.

This is middleware. We just gave it a cooler name.

The teams winning with MCP right now aren't the ones with the most servers connected. They're the ones who built a normalization layer between them. A thin contract that says: here's what a "company" looks like in this system, here's how dates work, here's the canonical shape of a contact.

Without that, you get an agent that works 80% of the time and fails silently the other 20%. Which is worse than failing loudly, because you ship bad data downstream and don't find out until a prospect replies confused.

The protocol is solved. The plumbing between protocols is where the real engineering lives.
remixes.cta: How are you handling schema mismatches between MCP servers in your stack?

remixes.label: middleware-history-repeats
remixes.hook: We've seen this movie before. SOAP. REST. GraphQL. Now MCP. The pattern is always the same: the protocol ships clean, then reality gets messy.
remixes.body:
We've seen this movie before. SOAP. REST. GraphQL. Now MCP. The pattern is always the same: the protocol ships clean, then reality gets messy.

MCP is elegant in demos. One server, one tool, one agent. Beautiful.

Then you wire four servers together and discover that none of them agree on what a "contact" is. One gives you an email and a name. Another gives you a domain and a role. A third returns a JSON blob with nested arrays that the fourth server chokes on.

So you write transformers. Validators. Retry logic. Error handlers for when Server B is down but Server A already committed.

Congratulations, you just reinvented enterprise middleware.

I'm not saying this is bad. Middleware exists because distributed systems are hard and someone has to own the translation layer. The problem is that nobody talks about this part. Every MCP tutorial shows the happy path. Connect a server, call a tool, get a result.

Nobody shows the 3am debugging session where your agent wrote to the CRM with a malformed phone number because the research server returned it with country code and the CRM server expected digits only.

MCP is powerful. But the unlock isn't the protocol. It's whoever builds the normalization layer that sits between all of them.

posts.title: Signal-to-sequence lag is the real leak
posts.hook: Your pipeline isn't slow because reps are slow. It's slow because signals sit in a queue for 72 hours before anyone acts on them.
posts.body:
Your pipeline isn't slow because reps are slow. It's slow because signals sit in a queue for 72 hours before anyone acts on them.

I built a signal router that watches for job posts, LinkedIn profile changes, and Reddit threads mentioning our category. When something fires, it writes to a SQLite table with a timestamp.

Then I measured the gap between signal_detected_at and first_outreach_at.

Average: 4.2 days.

The signal was fresh. The context was perfect. And by the time a human got to it, the prospect had already talked to two competitors.

So I automated the first touch. Not the whole sequence. Just the initial reply or connection request, drafted by an agent that reads the signal context and writes a response grounded in what actually triggered it.

Signal-to-sequence lag dropped to under 6 hours. Reply rates went up 3x. Not because the copy was better. Because timing is the variable that matters most and nobody tracks it.

If you're measuring pipeline velocity, start here. Not at close date. At the gap between when you knew and when you moved.
posts.cta: Have you ever measured how long signals sit before your team acts on them?

inspired_by.author: Kyle Coleman
inspired_by.summary: Most GTM teams are measuring pipeline velocity wrong. They track time-to-close but ignore signal-to-sequence lag — the gap between a buying signal firing and an SDR actually touching it. At Clari we found teams with sub-4-hour signal response rates close 31% more deals than teams responding in 24+ hours. The bottleneck isn't headcount. It's routing logic.

remixes.label: speed-kills-competitors
remixes.hook: We closed a deal last quarter purely because we responded 68 hours before the competitor did. Same signal. Same prospect. Different infrastructure.
remixes.body:
We closed a deal last quarter purely because we responded 68 hours before the competitor did. Same signal. Same prospect. Different infrastructure.

The signal was a job post for a "Revenue Operations Manager" at a Series B company. Classic buying signal. They're building the team to evaluate tools like ours.

Our system caught it at 9:14am. By 9:47am the prospect had a personalized email referencing the role, our relevant case study, and a calendar link. No human touched it until the reply came in.

The competitor's SDR found the same job post three days later during a manual LinkedIn prospecting session. By then our AE was already on a discovery call.

This isn't about AI or automation for its own sake. It's about compressing the gap between signal and action to near zero.

I measured our pipeline over 90 days. Deals where first outreach happened within 4 hours of signal detection closed at 3.1x the rate of deals where outreach took 48+ hours. Same reps. Same messaging. Same product.

The only variable was speed.

Most teams have the signals. They're sitting in Slack channels, email alerts, saved LinkedIn searches. The problem is the queue. Signals land, sit in a list, and wait for a human to context-switch into outbound mode.

The fix isn't hiring more reps. It's removing the queue entirely.
remixes.cta: What's your current lag time between detecting a buying signal and sending the first touch?

remixes.label: signal-rot-framework
remixes.hook: Buying signals have a half-life. After 24 hours, most of them are worthless.
remixes.body:
Buying signals have a half-life. After 24 hours, most of them are worthless.

I started tracking this after a frustrating quarter. We had great signal coverage. Job post alerts, tech stack monitoring, Reddit mentions, funding announcements. The data was flowing in.

But conversion rates were flat.

So I added a timestamp column. signal_detected_at and first_outreach_at. Then I plotted the gap against reply rates.

The data was brutal. Signals acted on within 2 hours had a 14% reply rate. Same signals acted on after 48 hours dropped to 3%. After 72 hours, statistically indistinguishable from cold outreach with no signal at all.

I call this signal rot. The information decays. A job post is most actionable the day it goes live, when the hiring manager is actively thinking about the problem. Three days later, they've already gotten 40 cold emails from people who saw the same post.

The fix wasn't better signals. We had plenty. The fix was eliminating the human queue between detection and action.

I built a router. Signal fires, gets classified by type, gets matched to a sequence template, gets enriched with context, and drafts outreach. A human reviews and hits send. Total time from detection to outbox: under 30 minutes.

The signals didn't change. The speed did. Reply rates doubled in the first month.

posts.title: Extended thinking changed my agent loops
posts.hook: Gave Claude extended thinking with 128K context on a refactor task. It rewrote 23 files in a single pass without hallucinating an import.
posts.body:
Gave Claude extended thinking with 128K context on a refactor task. It rewrote 23 files in a single pass without hallucinating an import.

That's not the interesting part.

The interesting part is what it did to my agent loop design. I used to break every task into tiny steps because models couldn't hold enough context to reason across files. Step 1: read the schema. Step 2: read the handler. Step 3: read the test. Step 4: now plan the change.

With extended thinking, I hand it the whole directory and say "refactor the auth layer to use middleware instead of per-route checks." It reads everything, thinks for 45 seconds, then executes.

My orchestration code got simpler. Fewer steps, fewer handoffs, fewer places for state to get corrupted between calls.

The tradeoff: cost. A single extended thinking call with full context runs 10-15x what a normal call costs. So I use it surgically. Complex multi-file changes get extended thinking. Simple edits get the fast path.

The pattern: treat extended thinking like a senior engineer you bring in for the hard problems. Not every ticket. The ones where context across the whole system matters.
posts.cta: Are you still breaking agent tasks into tiny steps, or have you started trusting longer context windows?

remixes.label: death-of-micro-steps
remixes.hook: I used to design agent loops like assembly lines. 12 discrete steps, each one isolated, each one simple enough that the model couldn't mess it up. That architecture is now obsolete.
remixes.body:
I used to design agent loops like assembly lines. 12 discrete steps, each one isolated, each one simple enough that the model couldn't mess it up. That architecture is now obsolete.

Here's what changed. Extended thinking with 128K context means the model can hold an entire codebase in working memory and reason across it. Not summarize it. Reason across it.

I gave it a refactor task last week. 23 files, interconnected types, shared imports. Old approach: read schema, then read handler, then read tests, then plan changes, then implement file by file. 12 tool calls minimum. Constant risk of the model forgetting what it read three steps ago.

New approach: load everything into context, turn on extended thinking, describe the end state. One pass. Zero hallucinated imports. Every type reference correct.

This changes agent architecture fundamentally. All those step-by-step orchestration frameworks people built? The ones with state machines and checkpoints and retry logic for each micro-step? They were compensating for a context limitation that no longer exists.

The new constraint isn't context size. It's knowing when to use a single powerful pass versus when to genuinely decompose. Some tasks are still better broken down. But the default has flipped. Start with one pass. Only decompose when you hit an actual reasoning boundary.

Simpler loops. Fewer failure points. Better results.

remixes.label: context-as-architecture
remixes.hook: The number of steps in your agent loop is a direct measure of how little you trust the model's context window.
remixes.body:
The number of steps in your agent loop is a direct measure of how little you trust the model's context window.

Think about it. Why do we break agent tasks into 8 or 12 micro-steps? Because six months ago, the model would lose track of what it read by step 4. So we engineered around the limitation. Read one file, summarize it, pass the summary forward, read the next file.

We were building compression pipelines for models that couldn't hold enough raw information to reason well.

Then 128K context with extended thinking shipped. And suddenly the bottleneck moved.

I tested this on a real refactor. 23 files, cross-cutting type changes, shared import chains. Loaded everything into context. Single pass. It tracked every import, updated every type reference, and didn't hallucinate a single dependency.

My old approach would have taken 15+ steps with checkpoints between each one. And it would have been more error-prone, because every handoff between steps is a chance to lose or corrupt information.

The implication for agent design: context window size is now an architectural input, not just a spec number. When context is small, you decompose aggressively. When context is large enough, you let the model reason holistically.

This means your agent framework needs to adapt based on the model's context capacity. Same task, different architecture depending on what model you're running it on.

The step count should shrink as the context grows. If it doesn't, you're over-engineering.

posts.title: RevOps is a trust problem
posts.hook: Every RevOps audit I've done starts the same way. Someone says "the data is in Salesforce" and then we open Salesforce and it isn't.
posts.body:
Every RevOps audit I've done starts the same way. Someone says "the data is in Salesforce" and then we open Salesforce and it isn't.

Or it's there but stale. Or duplicated. Or in a custom field that one rep created in 2023 and nobody else uses.

The instinct is to buy another tool. A dedup platform. An enrichment layer. A dashboard that "unifies" everything.

But the root cause isn't tooling. It's that nobody owns the data contract.

Who decides what "qualified" means in the stage field? Who enforces that phone numbers include country codes? Who notices when the Marketo sync breaks at 2am and 400 leads land without source attribution?

I started treating CRM data like code. Schema definitions in a repo. Validation rules that run on every write. A nightly cron that flags records that violate the contract and posts them to a Slack channel.

It's not glamorous work. Nobody tweets about writing a CRM validation script. But the downstream impact is everything. Your pipeline reports are only as honest as the data feeding them.

You can't analytics your way out of dirty data.

remixes.label: process-before-platform
remixes.hook: The most expensive CRM migration I've seen cost $180K and took 8 months. The data was just as bad in the new system.
remixes.body:
The most expensive CRM migration I've seen cost $180K and took 8 months. The data was just as bad in the new system.

Because they migrated the data without fixing the process that corrupted it in the first place.

Here's the pattern. Company has dirty CRM data. Leadership blames the tool. They buy a new CRM, or a dedup platform, or an enrichment layer. The vendor runs a one-time cleanup during migration. Data looks pristine on day one.

Six months later, same mess. Duplicate records. Stale fields. Custom objects nobody maintains. Contacts with three different email formats.

The problem was never the database. It was the fact that no one owns data quality as a continuous process.

In every RevOps audit I've done, the root cause comes back to the same three things. First, no clear ownership of who updates what. Second, no validation at the point of entry. Third, no regular audit cadence.

You can fix all three without buying anything. Define field ownership by role. Add required fields and picklists that prevent garbage at creation. Run a monthly query that flags records missing critical fields.

It's not exciting. There's no vendor demo. No dashboard to screenshot for the board. But it actually works.

The teams with clean CRM data don't have better tools. They have someone who decided that data quality is their job, not a feature request for the next platform purchase.
remixes.cta: How many tools has your org bought to fix what is fundamentally a process problem?

remixes.label: crm-archaeology
remixes.hook: I opened a client's Salesforce last month and found 47 custom fields created by former employees. Nobody knew what 39 of them meant.
remixes.body:
I opened a client's Salesforce last month and found 47 custom fields created by former employees. Nobody knew what 39 of them meant.

This is CRM archaeology. And every B2B company with more than 2 years of CRM history has it.

Here's how it happens. A rep joins, needs to track something specific to their workflow, creates a custom field. They leave. The field stays. Another rep joins, doesn't know the field exists, creates a slightly different version. Now you have "Deal Source" and "Lead Source Original" and "Source (Jake's)" all tracking the same concept with different values.

Multiply this across every team that touches the CRM. Marketing adds fields for campaign tracking. CS adds fields for health scores. Finance adds fields for billing. Nobody coordinates.

The result is a database where the schema itself is unreliable. You can't build reports because you don't know which field has the real data. You can't build automations because the field you're triggering on has 60% fill rate and the actual data lives somewhere else.

The fix is boring and unglamorous. Audit every custom field. Document who created it, what it's for, and who maintains it. Merge the duplicates. Delete the orphans. Then lock down field creation so it requires approval.

I've seen this single exercise improve reporting accuracy more than any BI tool purchase. Because the BI tool was never the bottleneck. The schema was.
remixes.cta: When was the last time someone audited the custom fields in your CRM?

posts.title: Cold email isn't dead, lazy email is
posts.hook: Ran a test last month. Same list, same offer, two different approaches.
posts.body:
Ran a test last month. Same list, same offer, two different approaches.

Version A: persona-based personalization. "As a VP of Marketing at a Series B company, you probably..." The template every outbound tool generates by default.

Version B: signal-based. We watched for companies posting specific job titles on LinkedIn, cross-referenced with tech stack changes from BuiltWith, and referenced the actual trigger in the first line. "Saw you're hiring a RevOps manager. Usually means the CRM is getting unwieldy."

Version A: 2.1% reply rate.
Version B: 11.4% reply rate.

The difference isn't copywriting talent. It's timing plus specificity. Version B proved we noticed something real about their business right now. Version A proved we had their job title in a spreadsheet.

The infrastructure to run Version B is heavier. You need a signal layer that watches events, an enrichment step that adds context, and a drafting step that references the trigger naturally. I run mine with a Python script, three API calls, and a SQLite queue.

Total cost per month: about $180 in API credits.

Cold email isn't dead. But if your personalization starts with "As a [title] at [company]" you're competing with every other tool that does the same thing.
posts.cta: What signals are you actually using to time your outbound?

remixes.hook: Personalization isn't what you say in the email. It's when you send it.
remixes.body:
Personalization isn't what you say in the email. It's when you send it.

I ran a head-to-head test last month. Same list of 400 contacts, same offer, two approaches.

Version A: classic personalization. Referenced their title, company stage, likely pain points. Well-written, specific to the persona. Sent on a Tuesday morning blast.

Version B: minimal personalization. Shorter copy. But triggered by a specific signal. We sent it within 4 hours of detecting a relevant job post, a tech stack change, or a competitor mention on their blog.

Version B crushed it. 3.4x higher reply rate. Not because the copy was better. Because the timing was relevant.

When someone posts a job for "Revenue Operations Manager," they're actively thinking about the problem you solve. An email that arrives in that window doesn't feel cold. It feels like good timing.

The same email arriving two weeks later, no matter how personalized, feels like every other cold outreach in their inbox.

We've been optimizing the wrong variable. The outbound industry spent five years perfecting personalization templates. Name, company, title, recent funding round, mutual connection. All of it helps marginally.

But none of it compensates for bad timing.

The highest-performing outbound teams I've seen aren't running the best templates. They're running the fastest signal-to-send infrastructure. The email is good enough. The timing is precise.
remixes.cta: What signal gives you the best timing advantage in your outbound?

remixes.label: persona-is-dead-long-live-signal
remixes.hook: Persona-based outbound is the default in every sales tool. It's also why your reply rates are declining every quarter.
remixes.body:
Persona-based outbound is the default in every sales tool. It's also why your reply rates are declining every quarter.

Every outbound platform starts the same way. Build a persona. VP Marketing, Series B, 50-200 employees, SaaS vertical. Write a template. Blast the list.

The problem: every other company using the same tools built the same persona and is sending the same template to the same people. Your prospect gets 12 emails a week that all start with "As a VP of Marketing at a growing SaaS company..."

Persona targeting tells you WHO to email. It tells you nothing about WHEN to email them or WHY right now.

I tested this. Same list, same offer. Version A used persona personalization. Version B used signal triggers. We watched for specific job posts, tech stack changes on BuiltWith, and category mentions on Reddit. Sent within hours of the signal.

Version B: 3.4x reply rate. And the replies were different. Instead of "not interested" or silence, we got "good timing, we're actually looking at this."

The signal told us something the persona couldn't: that this person is actively thinking about the problem right now.

Persona data is table stakes. Everyone has it. Signal timing is the differentiator, and most teams either don't have the infrastructure or don't have the speed to act on it.

The teams winning at outbound in 2026 aren't writing better emails. They're building faster signal pipes.

posts.title: Multi-agent handoff failures
posts.hook: Multi-agent systems don't fail loudly. They fail by quietly dropping context at the handoff.
posts.body:
Multi-agent systems don't fail loudly. They fail by quietly dropping context at the handoff.

I run an agent pipeline where Agent 1 researches a company, Agent 2 scores it, and Agent 3 drafts outreach. Clean separation of concerns. Looked great in the diagram.

Then I noticed the outreach was generic. Agent 3 was writing emails that could've been about any company.

The bug: Agent 1 returned a rich research object with 14 fields. Agent 2 consumed 6 of them for scoring. Agent 3 only received Agent 2's output, which was a score and a tier label. All the research context got dropped at the handoff.

Fix was simple. I added a passthrough field that carries the original research object through every agent in the chain, untouched. Each agent reads what it needs and passes the rest forward.

But I only found it because I logged the full input/output at every handoff and diffed what went in versus what came out.

If you're building multi-agent systems, instrument the handoffs first. Not the agents. The agents are usually fine. The space between them is where information dies.

Every production agent pipeline I've seen has this bug. Most teams just haven't looked yet.
posts.cta: How are you debugging the handoffs between agents in your pipelines?

inspired_by.author: Lilian Weng
inspired_by.summary: Every team I talk to is discovering the same thing: multi-agent systems fail silently at the handoff layer, not the task layer. Your agents complete their individual steps correctly but the context window between them is where the real bugs live. Published a framework for structuring agent handoffs that cut our error rate 60%.

remixes.label: detective-story
remixes.hook: I spent two hours debugging a prompt that was already perfect. The problem was three functions upstream.
remixes.body:
I spent two hours debugging a prompt that was already perfect. The problem was three functions upstream.

My outreach agent was writing bland emails. So I rewrote the prompt. Twice. Added examples. Added persona instructions. Still bland.

Then I logged the actual input the agent received. The company research from Agent 1 was a 4,000 token document. By the time it passed through the scoring layer, it was a JSON blob with a name, industry, and a confidence score. Every detail that would make the outreach specific was gone.

The scoring agent was doing its job correctly. It returned a clean, structured output. But "clean" meant it stripped the founder's podcast quotes, the recent product pivot, the hiring patterns. All the texture.

This is the trap with multi-agent architectures. Each agent optimizes for its own output contract. Nobody optimizes for what the downstream agent actually needs.

The fix was ugly but effective. I added a pass-through field called raw_context that bypasses the scoring schema entirely. The outreach agent now gets both the structured score and the original research. Emails went from 2% reply rate to 11%.

Your agents aren't broken. Your data contracts between them are.
remixes.cta: What's the most time you've spent debugging the wrong layer of your stack?

remixes.label: systems-thinking
remixes.hook: The diagram looks clean. Three agents, three steps, arrows pointing right. Then you ship it and the output is garbage.
remixes.body:
The diagram looks clean. Three agents, three steps, arrows pointing right. Then you ship it and the output is garbage.

Multi-agent pipelines have a compression problem nobody talks about. Every handoff is a lossy operation. Agent 1 knows everything. Agent 2 knows what Agent 1 decided to pass along. Agent 3 knows what survived two rounds of summarization.

By the time your final agent acts, it's working with a fraction of the original signal. Not because anything failed. Because each agent made rational decisions about what to include in its output.

I've started thinking about agent handoffs the way database engineers think about schema migrations. You need explicit contracts. What fields are required downstream? What gets lost if you compress? What's the minimum context that preserves the intent?

Three patterns that helped me: First, log every handoff payload for a week before optimizing. Second, have downstream agents flag when their input feels insufficient. Third, build a "context health" score that measures information loss across the pipeline.

The architecture diagram is the easy part. The hard part is making sure meaning survives the journey.

posts.title: Teacher to builder pipeline
posts.hook: A teacher shipped four products in nine months using Claude Code. That's not the story. The story is what made it possible.
posts.body:
A teacher shipped four products in nine months using Claude Code. That's not the story. The story is what made it possible.

Teachers already know how to break complex problems into sequential steps. They know how to write clear instructions for someone who doesn't have their context. They know how to debug when a student gives the wrong answer.

That's prompt engineering. They've been doing it for years, just with humans instead of models.

The gap used to be syntax. You needed to know React, or Python, or SQL before you could build anything. Coding agents collapsed that gap. Now the bottleneck is clarity of thought, not knowledge of frameworks.

I was a plumber before I was in tech. Same pattern. The trade taught me to diagnose systems, trace problems upstream, and fix root causes instead of symptoms. None of that required knowing JavaScript. But all of it translates directly to working with agents.

The next wave of builders isn't coming from CS programs. It's coming from people who already think in systems and just needed the syntax barrier removed.

The career pivot stories that land aren't "person learns to code." They're "person who already thinks like an engineer gets access to the tools."

The best prompt engineers I know never studied computer science. They studied education, law, and technical writing.

A former teacher I work with shipped four products in nine months. When I looked at his CLAUDE.md files and prompt structures, they read like lesson plans. Clear learning objectives. Scaffolded complexity. Checkpoints to verify understanding before moving forward.

posts.title: Dwell time is the new engagement
posts.hook: LinkedIn changed the algorithm and most people haven't adjusted.
posts.body:
LinkedIn changed the algorithm and most people haven't adjusted.

Dwell time now outweighs reactions. A post with 200 saves and low comments outperforms a post with 800 likes and fast scroll-throughs.

What this means practically: long, dense, tactical posts are back.

I tested this over the last 6 weeks. Short punchy takes (under 100 words) that used to perform well are getting 40-60% less reach. Long tactical breakdowns with real implementation details are getting 2-3x more impressions than the same format got three months ago.

The posts that work now are the ones people stop and read slowly. Save for later. Screenshot and send to a coworker.

So I changed my approach. Every post includes at least one of these: a specific workflow someone can copy, a real number from something I built, or a technical detail that takes a minute to absorb.

No more drive-by hot takes. No more "agree?" endings fishing for quick comments.

The play is to write posts worth reading twice. If someone has to pause and think about what you wrote, the algorithm notices.

This is actually better for practitioners. The people who build things have more to say. Now the algorithm rewards saying it.

I ran a 6-week experiment posting two types of LinkedIn content. The results were not subtle.

Group A: Short, punchy takes under 100 words. The kind that performed well 18 months ago. Clear hook, one insight, quick close.

Group B: Long, dense, tactical posts. 250 to 400 words. Step-by-step breakdowns, specific numbers, implementation details.

Group A averaged 40 to 60% less reach than my baseline. Group B averaged 2.3x more reach.

The reason is dwell time. LinkedIn's algorithm now weighs how long someone stays on your post more heavily than whether they tap the like button. A 300-word post with specifics keeps people reading for 45 to 90 seconds. A 60-word hot take gets a quick like and a scroll.

Saves matter more than reactions now too. A post with 200 saves and modest comments consistently outperforms a post with 800 likes.

The practical shift: stop optimizing for the quick dopamine hit. Write posts that people want to reference later. Include enough detail that someone could actually implement what you're describing.

Three structural changes I made: (1) Open with the result, not the philosophy. (2) Include at least one specific number or metric. (3) End with a question that requires thought, not just agreement.

The algorithm rewards depth now. Write like it.

posts.title: The honest build-in-public update
posts.hook: Build in public update that nobody wants to post: churn spiked, two deals stalled, and I rewrote the same feature three times this week.
posts.body:
Build in public update that nobody wants to post: churn spiked, two deals stalled, and I rewrote the same feature three times this week.

The churn spike came from a pricing change I was too confident about. Moved the free tier threshold down. Three customers who were on the edge churned within 48 hours. Should have grandfathered them. Didn't.

The stalled deals are both enterprise. Both want SOC 2. I don't have SOC 2. Building solo means you can ship fast but you can't manufacture compliance on demand.

The rewrite was my agent routing logic. Version 1 was a big if/else tree. Version 2 was an over-engineered class hierarchy. Version 3 is a simple dictionary lookup. Should have started there.

Here's what I'm learning: the build-in-public posts that get engagement are the wins. Shipped a feature. Hit a revenue number. Landed a client.

But the weeks that actually teach you something are the ones where everything breaks and you have to decide what to fix first with limited time and no team.

I fixed the pricing (grandfathered the three accounts, adjusted the threshold). The SOC 2 thing is a longer conversation. The routing logic finally works.

Not every week is a highlight reel. The unglamorous weeks are where the real building happens.

Week 37 of building in public. Here are the numbers I almost didn't share.

MRR dropped 18% this month. Three customers churned within 48 hours of a pricing change. I moved the free tier threshold down because the unit economics looked right on a spreadsheet. Forgot that the three accounts sitting just above the old threshold had been using the product daily for months. Should have grandfathered them. Didn't.

Two enterprise deals are frozen. Both want SOC 2 compliance before signing. I don't have it. I knew this was coming and punted it because the engineering lift felt too big for the stage. Now it's costing me real revenue.

Rewrote the same feature three times this week. Not because the code was wrong. Because I kept changing the scope based on feedback from different users who want different things. Classic founder trap of trying to build for everyone at once.

The build-in-public posts that get engagement are the wins. The launches, the revenue milestones, the screenshots of dashboards going up and to the right. Nobody wants to post this version.

But this version is the actual job. Pricing mistakes you can't undo. Compliance gaps that block deals. Scope creep from trying to make everyone happy.

The lesson from all three: decisions I delayed because they were uncomfortable became the most expensive decisions of the month.

remixes.label: pattern-recognition
remixes.hook: Every build-in-public failure I had this month traces back to the same root cause: avoiding discomfort.
remixes.body:
Every build-in-public failure I had this month traces back to the same root cause: avoiding discomfort.

Churn spiked because I changed pricing without having the uncomfortable conversation with affected customers first. I knew three accounts were right on the edge. Reaching out to them before the change would have taken 30 minutes and three emails. I skipped it because I didn't want to justify the new pricing one-on-one.

Two enterprise deals stalled because I've been avoiding the SOC 2 conversation for months. Every quarter I look at the compliance checklist, estimate the effort, and decide it's not urgent yet. Meanwhile, real buyers are telling me it's the only thing blocking their signature.

Rewrote a feature three times because I didn't want the discomfort of telling two users "no, this isn't what we're building." Instead I tried to build for both of them and built for neither.

The pattern is obvious in hindsight. The uncomfortable thing is almost always the correct thing. The 30-minute email. The hard scope decision. The compliance investment that feels premature.

Building in public usually means sharing results. But the more useful share is the decision-making pattern that produced those results. Mine has a clear bias: I default to the comfortable option and it costs me every time.

I'm working on fixing that. Starting with the SOC 2 project I should have started six months ago.

posts.title: 2 engineers replaced 12 labelers
posts.hook: A team replaced a 12-person data labeling pipeline with 2 engineers and an agent workflow. The part people miss: the 2 engineers are doing harder work than before.
posts.body:
A team replaced a 12-person data labeling pipeline with 2 engineers and an agent workflow. The part people miss: the 2 engineers are doing harder work than before.

Before, those engineers managed people who labeled data. Hiring, QA, shift scheduling, dispute resolution. Project management with a labeling skin.

Now those same engineers are writing structured output schemas, building evaluation harnesses, debugging edge cases where the model confidently labels something wrong, and designing the feedback loop that catches drift before it corrupts downstream models.

The headcount dropped. The skill requirement went up.

I see this same pattern in GTM. I replaced manual lead research (3 hours per account) with an agent pipeline that enriches, scores, and drafts in 4 minutes. But now I spend that saved time building better scoring logic, refining the signals that trigger outreach, and auditing output quality.

The work didn't disappear. It moved up the stack.

Every "AI replaced X people" story has a hidden second chapter: the remaining people are now doing work that requires deeper judgment, and if they can't level up, the system produces confidently wrong output at scale.

Automation without quality loops is just faster mistakes.

Automation doesn't eliminate hard work. It concentrates it.

A team I know replaced a 12-person data labeling pipeline with 2 engineers and an agent workflow. Leadership saw the headcount reduction. What they missed was the job transformation.

Before automation, those engineers were project managers with a technical title. They hired labelers, scheduled shifts, ran QA spot checks, resolved disputes about ambiguous labels. The work was tedious but well-understood.

After automation, those same engineers are doing work that barely existed two years ago. Writing structured output schemas that handle edge cases the model has never seen. Building evaluation harnesses that catch subtle labeling drift. Designing feedback loops between the model's confidence scores and human review triggers.

The old role had a playbook. The new role requires inventing the playbook.

This is the pattern I keep seeing across every team that automates with AI. The total hours of work decrease. The difficulty per hour increases. The remaining humans need to be significantly more skilled than before.

Companies are celebrating the cost savings without investing in the skill upgrade. They kept 2 engineers instead of 12 labelers but didn't change the job title, the compensation, or the expectations. Those 2 engineers are now doing senior ML engineering work at mid-level project manager pay.

Automation doesn't make work easier. It makes the remaining work harder. Plan for that.

The job description said "data labeling manager." The actual job is now ML systems engineer. Same role, same pay, completely different skill set.

A team replaced their 12-person labeling pipeline with an agent workflow. Two engineers remained. On paper, they saved 10 headcount. In practice, they created two of the hardest jobs in the company.

The old job: manage people who label data. Hire, train, QA, schedule shifts, resolve disagreements about edge cases. You could learn the job in a few months. The complexity was logistical, not technical.

The new job: design the schema the agent uses to label. Build evaluation harnesses that catch when the model drifts. Write the rules for when confidence is too low and a human needs to review. Debug failures that don't look like failures because the output is formatted correctly but semantically wrong.

The hiring implication is massive. The talent pool for "manage a team of labelers" is large. The talent pool for "build and maintain an AI labeling system's quality infrastructure" is tiny. And the compensation gap between those two roles is significant.

Most companies I see automate the headcount but don't update the job description. They're asking mid-level operations people to do senior ML engineering and wondering why quality is dropping.

When you automate a process, the first question shouldn't be "how many people can we cut?" It should be "can the remaining people do the harder job that's left?"
